venues.d: The jeweller's Milanese house — a hidden 18th-century palazzo with a vast private garden, a cul-de-sac from Via Montenapoleone.
A serene former Renaissance convent in the heart of the fashion quarter — cloistered gardens and the surest hands in Milan.
Four linked 18th-century palazzi on a discreet backstreet beside La Scala — the city's only Forbes Five-Star.
A Ferragamo-family house built around Milan's oldest Baroque seminary courtyard — the address of the moment.
Mr Armani's own vision of stay — greige calm and 'stay with Armani' service on Via Manzoni.

venues.n: Hotel Principe di Savoia, Dorchester Collection
venues.d: A neoclassical grand dame on Piazza della Repubblica — old-Milan splendour on a generous scale.
Milan's historic grand hotel since 1863 — Verdi's home for decades, steps from La Scala.
A members'-club-style house of quiet exclusivity — the Cipriani sense of ease, brought to central Milan.
A light-filled palazzo on the edge of Brera — marble, French windows and one of Milan's largest hotel spas.
A fairy-tale Art Nouveau castle near the Giardini — theatrical, romantic and a little out of the ordinary.
A sleek, design-led newcomer in the towers of Porta Nuova — contemporary Milan at its most current.

venues.n: Excelsior Hotel Gallia, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A 1932 Art Deco landmark by Centrale station — Milan's largest hotel spa and a celebrated rooftop over the city.
A sleek vertical hotel in the towers of Porta Nuova — contemporary Milan, with a Michelin-starred kitchen inside.
A serene, all-white design boutique built around a courtyard — 43 rooms of quiet Milanese taste.
A polished, well-run house a minute from the Duomo — location above all.
A design hotel tucked right beside the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II — you cannot stay more central.
A quirky, sport-and-vintage-themed townhouse hotel with real personality, near Porta Romana.
A restored canal-side house on the Naviglio Grande — a rare pocket of calm on the water.
Milan's only three-star — Italy's most-decorated chef, on the top floor of the MUDEC museum.

venues.a: Porta Venezia (Fondazione Luigi Rovati, Corso Venezia)
venues.d: Aprea's elegant two-star atop the Rovati foundation — contemporary Italian with a Neapolitan soul.

venues.n: Il Luogo di Aimo e Nadia
venues.d: A Milanese institution — Negrini and Pisani carrying forward one of Italy's great kitchens.
The Capitaneo brothers' assured two-star — refined, personal cooking near the Duomo.
Carlo Cracco's grand dining room inside the Galleria itself — the most glamorous address in Milan.
Matias Perdomo's playful, boundary-pushing tasting menu in an intimate townhouse room.
Andrea Berton's clean, modern cooking in the glass towers of Porta Nuova — broths and clarity are his signature.
Claudio Sadler's long-held star — classical technique and Milanese elegance, quietly enduring.
Viviana Varese's bold, sustainability-minded cooking — one of the city's most personal kitchens.
Italy's first starred Japanese restaurant — the room that proved sushi could be haute in Milan.
Takeshi Iwai's ambitious Japanese-European tasting room in the Porta Nuova towers.
Norbert Niederkofler's radically seasonal 'Cook the Mountain' ethos, on a rooftop above the centre.
Europe's first vegetarian restaurant to win a star — Pietro Leemann's meditative, plant-led cooking.
A polished modern-Milanese room with a cocktail-bar heart — refined cooking, easy warmth.
A confident hotel-restaurant star in Porta Nuova — contemporary Italian with technical polish.
Roberto Di Pinto's personal, southern-rooted cooking — one of the city's warmest starred rooms.
A newly-starred room of very personal cooking and live piano each evening — raw material, technique, hospitality.
Fabio Abbattista's 2024 debut, starred within a year — precise, well-travelled contemporary cooking.
Milan's glamorous seafood temple — oysters, crustaceans and the catch of the day, done with real flair.
Cesare Battisti's love letter to Lombard cooking — the yellow risotto alla milanese, done properly.
Diego Rossi's cult trattoria — offal, Milanese classics and Italian regional cooking, done with real conviction.
A beloved family-run Calabrian trattoria — 'nduja, fresh pasta and southern warmth, unchanged for decades.
Generous, homely Abruzzese cooking in enormous portions — a great-value Milan institution.
Milan's long-loved Sri Lankan and Indian table — the name means 'happy land', and it delivers.
Modern Italian cooking in the revived Palazzo del Ghiaccio complex — creative and good value.
Serious, fiery Sichuan cooking — a reminder that some of Milan's best value is well beyond the centre.
The best pizza in Milan — Neapolitan rounds, fried, padellino and gourmet slices, with a wine list to match.
The pizza-and-cocktails original that redefined the Milanese evening — great pies, better drinks.
Honest, well-made Neapolitan pizza across the city — a dependable, everyday favourite.
Milan's most elegant historic pasticceria — a Prada-owned jewel-box for coffee and pastries under the Galleria.
A modern Milanese bakery beloved for its brioche and pastries — the city's best morning ritual.

The vast pink-Candoglia-marble Gothic cathedral that took nearly six centuries to build is the emotional centre of Milan and the natural first stop for a multi-generational family. Book a skip-the-line entry so grandparents move straight in from the piazza rather than queueing in the sun.

You walk among 3,400 statues, spires and flying buttresses in Candoglia marble, with the Alps on the horizon on a clear day and the golden Madonnina overhead. Take the lift rather than the 251 steps for older relatives and small children, and go late afternoon for the light.

venues.n: The Last Supper (Il Cenacolo), Santa Maria delle Grazie
venues.d: Leonardo da Vinci's fragile 1490s mural survives on the refectory wall of a Dominican convent, seen by only small timed groups for 15 minutes at a time. Tickets vanish months ahead, so this is exactly the sort of unlock a concierge should secure well before you travel.

The soaring 1877 glass-and-iron arcade linking the Duomo to La Scala is both a monument and the world's oldest luxury shopping mall, home to the original Prada boutique, Louis Vuitton, and the historic Camparino bar. Spin your heel on the mosaic bull for luck, then let the family browse in cool shade.

Opened in 1778, La Scala is the most storied opera house on earth, where Verdi and Puccini premiered and where a box for the season opener is one of Milan's true social currencies. Pair a performance with the adjoining museum for the daytime members of a multi-gen group.

The grid of Via Montenapoleone, Via della Spiga, Via Sant'Andrea and Via Manzoni is the densest concentration of maison flagships in the world — Armani, Prada, Versace, Dolce & Gabbana, Bottega, Hermes. Ask for private appointments and after-hours boutique openings; this is the reason many UHNI travellers come to Milan at all.

The vast 15th-century Sforza fortress holds a cluster of civic museums including Michelangelo's unfinished final work, the Rondanini Pietà. The scale and open courtyards make it easy for children and grandparents to wander at their own pace before Parco Sempione behind it.

Milan's greatest picture gallery, with Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, Mantegna's foreshortened Dead Christ and Piero della Francesca's Montefeltro Altarpiece. Compact enough for one focused visit, and set inside the atmospheric artists' quarter for lunch afterwards.

The cobbled bohemian quarter around the Pinacoteca, with its botanical garden, art shops, antiques and candlelit trattorias, is the most romantic part of central Milan to stroll after dark. Quiet, walkable and discreet — ideal for an evening away from the crowds.

A perfectly preserved 19th-century aristocrat's house-museum steps from the fashion streets, its most famous piece Pollaiuolo's Portrait of a Young Woman. Intimate and rarely crowded — a refined pause between boutique appointments.

The Bagatti Valsecchi brothers built a lavish neo-Renaissance home in the 1880s and filled it with genuine 15th- and 16th-century art and furniture, then lived in it. One of Europe's best-preserved historic house-museums, and a hidden gem in the middle of the Quadrilatero.

Milan's museum of 20th-century Italian art sits inside the Palazzo dell'Arengario on Piazza del Duomo, its spiral ramp opening onto Futurist masterpieces and a fourth-floor window framing the cathedral. The rooftop restaurant Giacomo Arengario has cathedral views for lunch.

Three interconnected palazzi facing La Scala hold a superb collection of 19th- and 20th-century Italian art, from Canova bas-reliefs to Boccioni. Beautifully restored, air-conditioned and calm — a civilised refuge in the very centre.

Rem Koolhaas/OMA transformed a 1910s distillery into a striking contemporary art campus, complete with a gold-leaf-clad 'Haunted House' and Wes Anderson's jewel-box Bar Luce. A design pilgrimage that appeals to the younger generation as much as serious collectors.

A colossal former industrial hangar showing ambitious contemporary art, anchored by Anselm Kiefer's permanent 'The Seven Heavenly Palaces' — seven leaning concrete towers up to 19 metres tall. Free to enter and genuinely awe-inspiring for all ages.

The Naviglio Grande and Naviglio Pavese canals, part of a system Leonardo helped engineer, are now a lively waterside quarter of aperitivo bars, vintage shops and the monthly antiques market. Charming to walk by day; for UHNI travellers a private canal-side dinner or a quiet aperitivo away from the student crowd works best.

Milan's gleaming business district around Piazza Gae Aulenti is crowned by the Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri's award-winning 'vertical forest' towers dressed in thousands of trees. A striking counterpoint to old Milan and a favourite with design-minded younger travellers.

This vast 19th-century cemetery is an open-air museum of Italian funerary sculpture, with extravagant Art Nouveau and Art Deco tombs of Milan's great industrial families. Solemn, uncrowded and photographically extraordinary — a quietly moving hidden gem.

The pedestrian Corso Como is home to the legendary concept store 10 Corso Como, founded by Carla Sozzani — a pioneering blend of fashion, design, gallery, bookshop and courtyard café. A one-stop distillation of Milanese taste for the shopping-focused.

Italy's leading museum of design and architecture, set in the elegant Palazzo dell'Arte on the edge of Parco Sempione, with the permanent Italian Design Museum and a rooftop restaurant. Essential for anyone who cares about how Milan became the world's design capital.

One of the oldest churches in Milan, founded by the city's patron Saint Ambrose in the 4th century, its austere Romanesque form a world away from the Gothic Duomo. A serene, deeply historic stop with beautiful golden mosaics.

venues.n: Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore & Colonne di San Lorenzo
venues.d: An early-Christian basilica fronted by 16 Roman columns — the finest surviving ancient Roman ruin in Milan — with the exquisite Cappella di Sant'Aquilino and its 4th-century mosaics inside. The colonnade square is a lively evening gathering spot in the Ticinese.

A 1930s rationalist villa with pool and tennis court, restored by the FAI and used as a film set (I Am Love, House of Gucci), offering a rare glimpse into moneyed Milanese domestic life between the wars. Its garden café is a discreet, elegant lunch.

Founded by Cardinal Federico Borromeo in 1618, this gallery holds Caravaggio's Basket of Fruit, Raphael's cartoon for the School of Athens, and pages of Leonardo's Codex Atlanticus. A serious, uncrowded collection a short walk from the Duomo.

venues.n: Museo Nazionale Scienza e Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci
venues.d: Italy's largest science and technology museum, with galleries of machines built from Leonardo's drawings plus a real submarine and vintage aircraft. The most reliable crowd-pleaser in the city for children and teenagers.

Milan's grand central park unfurls behind the Sforza Castle to the Napoleonic Arch of Peace, with the Torre Branca observation tower for aerial views. Green, walkable space for grandparents and children between the museums.

A refined day-spa set in a historic building beside a stretch of the old Spanish city walls, with pools, saunas and a tram-carriage relaxation room. A restorative half-day for the adults while the family shops or sightsees.

venues.n: Chiesa di San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore
venues.d: Nicknamed the 'Sistine Chapel of Milan', this modest 16th-century church interior is entirely covered in luminous frescoes by Bernardino Luini and his school. Free, uncrowded and utterly unexpected — a true hidden gem near the Last Supper.

venues.n: Corso Vittorio Emanuele II & San Babila
venues.d: The pedestrian high street running from the Duomo to Piazza San Babila is Milan's mainstream shopping spine — Italian and international brands, department stores and cafes. Useful for the family's everyday buys while serious shopping happens in the Quadrilatero next door.

La Rinascente, Italy's landmark department store beside the Duomo, has a seventh-floor terrace of food counters and bars looking straight onto the cathedral spires. A convenient, glamorous perch for a break with unbeatable views.

venues.n: Fondazione Nicola Trussardi & Palazzo Marino (Piazza della Scala)
venues.d: The elegant Piazza della Scala, anchored by the 16th-century Palazzo Marino (Milan's city hall) and a Leonardo monument, is one of the city's most photogenic squares. A graceful pause between La Scala and the shopping streets.

The Rotonda della Besana is a serene 18th-century circular arcaded courtyard, once a cemetery, now a tranquil green enclosure with a baroque chapel. A calm, little-known spot for a quiet stroll away from any crowd.

Once a working-class 'island' cut off by the railway, Isola is now Milan's coolest quarter — independent boutiques, natural-wine bars and design studios in the shadow of the Bosco Verticale. Best explored on foot for a feel of contemporary Milanese life.

Corso Venezia is lined with grand Liberty-style (Italian Art Nouveau) palaces and leads to the leafy Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli. An elegant residential quarter with fine dining and the city's Natural History Museum for children.

The pre-dinner ritual of a Negroni or Milano-Torino with generous snacks was effectively invented here — Campari was born in Milan. For UHNI travellers, a reserved table at a rooftop bar such as Terrazza Aperol or a hotel bar beats the crowded street scene.

Camparino in Galleria (1915) is the birthplace of the Campari ritual, while Pasticceria Cova on Via Montenapoleone has served Milanese society since 1817. Both are elegant, vegetarian-friendly stops for coffee, pastries and people-watching.

Under an hour by train or car, Lake Como delivers the classic Italian lakes fantasy — Bellagio's terraced gardens, Villa del Balbianello, Villa Carlotta and George Clooney's Laglio. Arrange a private boat and a villa lunch; this is the single most requested escape from Milan.

Less than an hour away, Bergamo's walled Città Alta is a beautifully intact medieval-Renaissance hill town reached by an 1887 funicular, crowned by the Piazza Vecchia and the Colleoni Chapel. Its Venetian walls are UNESCO-listed and its restaurants excellent and unhurried.

Around 90 minutes away, Lake Maggiore's Borromean Islands hold the baroque Palazzo Borromeo on Isola Bella, its terraced gardens roamed by white peacocks, and the fishing village of Isola dei Pescatori. Grander and quieter than Como, ideal for a private-boat day.

Less than an hour south, this Carthusian charterhouse commissioned in 1396 by the Visconti dukes is one of the great masterpieces of Italian Gothic-Renaissance architecture, its facade a riot of marble sculpture. Serene, still a working monastery, and beautifully off the mainstream tourist trail.

About an hour east toward Lake Iseo, Franciacorta is Italy's answer to Champagne — rolling vineyards producing traditional-method sparkling wine, with elegant cellars offering private tastings and lunches. A refined, adult day out for oenophiles.

The medieval city on the Ticino river has one of Europe's oldest universities (1361), a distinctive covered bridge and towered skyline. Easily paired with the Certosa for a full, unhurried day away from Milan's bustle.
Milan's highest-ranked bar — a food-music-and-cocktails concept of rare coherence, and the world's Highest Climber of its year.
A password-and-membership speakeasy of quiet excellence — one of Italy's most consistently ranked bars.
The birthplace of the Milanese aperitivo — a Liberty-style bar under the Galleria, where Campari itself was born.
The birthplace of the Negroni Sbagliato — an unchanging 1960s institution and the temple of Milanese aperitivo.
An aperitivo terrace looking straight onto the Duomo — the most Milanese spritz there is.
Dsquared2's rooftop bar and pools above the old Enel building — glamour, a spritz and a sweep over the skyline.
The pizza-and-cocktails original — a Brera room where the drinks are as serious as the pies.
A tiny, cult tiki-and-molecular bar that has long featured among the world's best — theatre in a glass.
